title: Baby whale surprises scientists
summary:
The 2027 baby season for North Atlantic right whales has officially begun. The calving season lasts from November through April, and it is a particularly important stretch of time because the species is classified as critically endangered by the IUCN Red List. Scientists are closely monitoring these baleen whales because their numbers are so low. Yet even with all of that watching, one whale managed to keep a secret until September. Experts spotted a known female and her previously unidentified calf from last calving season near Anticosti Island, Quebec, Canada, according to the New England Aquarium.

The 38-year-old female right whale is called Silt. In addition to being a mother, Silt is also a grandmother and great-grandmother, and the new calf is her sixth baby known to scientists. 'Silt managed to fly under the radar of survey teams throughout the spring and summer,' according to the aquarium. Although scientists do not know exactly when or where her calf was born, she was briefly seen in the southeastern United States calving grounds in February, so it is possible the calf was born there.

More North Atlantic right whales are always good news. They are one of the most endangered large whales, and they are vulnerable to ship collisions and fishing gear entanglement. Almost exactly a year ago, scientists were happy to report that the species is showing signs of slowly rebounding. The 2024 estimate of around 384 North Atlantic right whales represents a 2.1 percent increase from the 2023 estimate. 'The population increase is really good news, and so far, what we've seen in 2025 is also good news,' New England Aquarium senior scientist Heather Pettis told Popular Science in October 2025. But she added that 384 individual whales is still incredibly low, and that scientists are cautiously optimistic because injuries from human activities continue.
why_it_matters: Every new right whale calf helps a critically endangered species recover, and protecting whales from ships and fishing gear matters for the whole ocean.

background_read: North Atlantic right whales are baleen whales, which filter tiny food from seawater instead of hunting with teeth.
They are critically endangered, so scientists watch them closely, especially during the calving season from November through April, when mothers give birth to new calves.
Each new calf matters because the whole population is very small, and the whales can be hurt by ship collisions and fishing gear.
Survey teams track known whales by sight, but a mother and calf can still go unseen for months if they stay away from the usual survey areas.
